Channels: Paid, Owned, and Earned

What does each channel trade between control, cost, and credibility? A working model for the choice every go-to-market plan eventually forces.

On the second Tuesday of March, Rhea Bhandari sat in a glass-walled conference room on the fourth floor of Kamini Home, a Bengaluru-based direct-to-consumer furnishings company, staring at a marketing plan she had drafted twice and rejected twice. Kamini Home sold hand-block-printed bedsheets, cushion covers, and table linen through its own website and a modest footprint of twenty-two shop-in-shop counters inside large-format retail stores. The company had just closed a ₹14 crore Series A, and the board wanted a growth plan that would take monthly revenue from ₹85 lakh to ₹2.4 crore within nine months. Rhea, who had joined eleven months earlier as the company's first dedicated growth lead, had exactly one number pinned above her desk: customer acquisition cost, or CAC, currently running at ₹740 per paying customer against an average order value of ₹1,650. The instinct in the room, voiced loudest by the co-founder who controlled the performance-marketing budget, was to simply spend more on Meta and Google ads — if ₹18 lakh a month in paid spend was producing 2,400 orders, then ₹40 lakh should produce something close to double that. Rhea did not think the arithmetic would hold, and she suspected the deeper problem was that Kamini Home had built almost no channel other than paid media: no email list worth mentioning, a dormant Instagram account with 9,000 followers, and not a single meaningful piece of press or word-of-mouth momentum despite three years of genuinely well-reviewed product. If she was right and paid spend alone could not carry the company to ₹2.4 crore without CAC rising past the point of profitability, she would need to persuade a board eager for speed to instead fund two channels that would take longer to show results and that she could not fully control. Getting this wrong in either direction — over-investing in paid until margins collapsed, or under-investing in paid while owned and earned channels were still too immature to carry volume — would cost Kamini Home a growth quarter it could not easily repeat with investor patience already finite.

The idea

A channel, in go-to-market terms, is any route through which a company gets in front of a potential customer and moves them toward a purchase or a signup. The paid–owned–earned framework sorts every such route into three families based on a single underlying question: who controls the message and the placement, and what did the company give up to get there? A paid channel is one where the company buys exposure directly — search ads, social ads, sponsorships, influencer fees, affiliate commissions — and can dictate the message, the audience, and the timing in exchange for cash, on a schedule that stops the moment the spending stops. An owned channel is a property the company itself controls indefinitely without paying a third party for access each time — its website, its email list, its app, its blog, its own social accounts — built over time and, once built, nearly free to reuse. An earned channel is exposure the company did not pay for and does not control — press coverage, word of mouth, organic search rankings driven by others linking to the site, customer reviews, a product going viral on social media because users shared it unprompted — granted by other people's independent judgment rather than purchased outright.

The three-way split has no single inventor and no fixed birthdate; it crystallized gradually inside marketing and public-relations practice through the 1990s and 2000s as digital channels multiplied and practitioners needed a vocabulary for comparing a Google ad, a company blog post, and a newspaper mention on the same terms, and it was popularized in its current paid-owned-earned phrasing by marketing and media commentators — notably writers at Forrester Research and in advertising trade press — around 2009 to 2011, as brands began building their own websites and social accounts at scale for the first time and needed to explain why those investments were not simply "free advertising." The problem it solves is a persistent category error: treating every way of reaching customers as interchangeable, fungible with a single "marketing budget" line, when in fact each family behaves by fundamentally different economics, timelines, and risk profiles. The sentence Rhea could say in that board meeting without sounding glib was this: paid buys you reach right now in exchange for cash and no credibility bump, owned compounds slowly into a nearly-free asset you fully control, and earned is the cheapest and most credible of the three but the one you can least command on demand.

One sentence for the room: every channel trades among control, cost, and credibility — you can usually buy two of the three, never all three at once.

How it actually works

Practitioners who use the framework well do not stop at labelling a channel paid, owned, or earned; they walk through four steps that people who merely know the vocabulary tend to skip. The first step is mapping every current and candidate channel onto the triangle honestly, including the channels a company would rather not admit are underdeveloped — Rhea's map showed paid search and paid social fully built, owned reduced to a transactional website and an email list she had never actually emailed, and earned essentially at zero, since three years of good reviews had never been systematically asked for, collected, or amplified. The second step is pricing each channel not by its sticker cost but by its fully-loaded cost per acquired customer, because a channel that looks cheap per click can be expensive per customer if its conversion rate is poor, and a channel that looks free, like organic social, is never actually free once the labour of running it is counted. The third and most often skipped step is estimating the lag between investing in a channel and that channel producing volume: paid channels respond within days, owned channels — an email list, a blog with search traffic — take months to compound, and earned channels are the slowest and least predictable of all, sometimes taking a year of consistent product quality and customer delight before word of mouth becomes a measurable share of new signups. The fourth step, and the one that separates a genuine channel strategy from a wish list, is deciding the sequencing and the funding split deliberately, in writing, with an explicit view on which channel is meant to carry the business now, which is being seeded for eighteen months from now, and how the three will eventually reinforce each other — paid traffic that lands on a genuinely good product creates the reviews and referrals that become earned reach, and an engaged email list, itself an owned asset, becomes a testing ground for messages a company later spends money amplifying through paid.

Rhea's version of step one looked almost embarrassing on a whiteboard: of Kamini Home's roughly 2,400 monthly orders, 2,150 traced to paid search and paid social, 200 to direct visits from the email list and repeat customers, and fewer than 50 to anything earned — a stray mention in a regional lifestyle blog and scattered word-of-mouth she could not even measure precisely. A company that leaned that hard on one corner of the triangle was not running a channel strategy; it was running a single channel with two decorative afterthoughts, and every rupee of growth the board wanted would have to come from a channel whose cost per customer, she suspected, did not stay flat as spend increased.

A worked example

Rhea built the arithmetic the board needed to see. Kamini Home's paid channel, in the month just closed, spent ₹18,00,000 to produce 2,150 orders — a blended customer acquisition cost of ₹837 per order once she separated new customers from the modest share of repeat buyers who clicked a retargeting ad. Average order value was ₹1,650, and gross margin on that revenue ran at 54%, meaning each order contributed roughly ₹891 in gross profit before marketing cost. Against a CAC of ₹837, that left a contribution margin of only ₹54 per order after paid acquisition cost — a razor's edge that made the "just spend more" instinct dangerous rather than merely aggressive, because Meta and Google auctions do not hold cost-per-click flat as a bidder increases budget; a company bidding for a larger share of the same finite audience typically pays a rising marginal price for each additional customer once it has already captured the cheapest, most easily converted segment of that audience.

The second pass is the one that changed the room. Rhea did not assume orders would simply double if spend doubled; she used Kamini Home's own auction data, which showed cost-per-click rising roughly 18% each time weekly budget rose past the point where the campaign was already capturing the most responsive searchers, a pattern common enough in paid search and social auctions that experienced performance marketers plan for it explicitly. Modelling that curve, doubling spend to ₹36 lakh produced an estimated 3,650 orders rather than 4,300, pushing CAC to ₹986 — above the ₹891 gross profit per order — which meant every additional order at that spend level actively lost the company ₹95, for a projected net contribution of minus ₹3,46,750 in the scenario the co-founder had wanted to fund. The arithmetic did not say paid spend was wrong; it said paid spend alone, at the volumes the board wanted, would cross into unprofitable territory well before ₹2.4 crore in monthly revenue was reached, and that the shortfall had to come from somewhere with a different cost curve — which is exactly what owned and earned channels offer, since their marginal cost per additional customer falls rather than rises as they mature.

The nuances a learner must sit with

Owned is not free, only front-loaded

The costliest mistake in how people talk about owned channels is calling them free. Kamini Home's email list and blog would cost real money and real time to build — content, design, a lifecycle-marketing hire — but that cost is paid once, largely up front, and then amortized across every future email sent to a list that keeps growing, whereas paid cost recurs every single time a customer is reached. The distinction that matters is not free-versus-paid but front-loaded-versus-recurring.

Earned cannot be scheduled, only invited

A company can create the conditions that make earned reach more likely — a product worth talking about, a review-request flow at the right post-purchase moment, a founder visible enough to be quoted by a journalist — but it cannot buy a guaranteed volume of word-of-mouth mentions the way it can buy a guaranteed volume of ad impressions. Teams that set a quarterly earned-media "target" the way they set a paid-media target are usually about to be disappointed, because the honest unit of earned strategy is effort and conditions, not committed output.

Paid and performance marketing are not synonyms

Paid channels include brand sponsorships and offline advertising that are bought but not directly measurable in the way a Google Ads dashboard is; people who use "paid" to mean only performance marketing miss that a billboard or a cricket-season television spot is also paid, just with a different, slower attribution problem.

The framework describes acquisition, not everything

Paid, owned, and earned classify how a customer first arrives or is reminded to return; it says nothing directly about product quality, pricing, or retention, and a company can have a beautifully balanced channel mix acquiring customers into a product that then fails to keep them. The triangle is a lens on the top of the funnel, not a complete growth strategy.

The boundaries blur in practice, and that is normal

An influencer paid a flat fee is paid media; the same influencer posting unprompted because they genuinely liked the product is earned; a company reposting that unprompted post on its own Instagram account is now using an earned asset through an owned channel. A referred customer clicking a paid retargeting ad after hearing about the brand from a friend blends earned discovery with paid conversion. Practitioners who insist every channel must sit cleanly in one bucket are fighting the framework rather than using it.

Cost per acquisition is not flat within a channel

As Rhea's own numbers showed, the marginal cost of the next customer through a paid channel typically rises as spend increases and the easiest-to-convert audience is exhausted; owned and earned channels tend to show the opposite pattern, with marginal cost falling as the list, the content library, or the reputation compounds. A channel decision made on today's average cost, ignoring where each channel sits on its own cost curve, will consistently over-fund paid and under-fund the other two.

Attribution across channels is genuinely hard

A customer who first heard of Kamini Home from a friend, later saw a retargeting ad, and finally converted after opening a welcome email touched all three channel families, and standard last-click analytics tools will credit only the email or the ad, systematically undercounting earned and owned influence. A thoughtful newcomer should ask which channel gets credit in their company's reporting and should distrust any single-touch attribution model applied uncritically to a multi-channel journey.

What the framework cannot tell you

It cannot tell a team which specific paid platform, which specific content topic, or which specific press outlet to pursue — those are execution choices one level below the framework. It also cannot tell a company how much total marketing budget it should have; it only helps allocate a budget decided elsewhere. Treating the triangle as a complete planning tool, rather than one input alongside unit economics and company stage, is a reliable way to misuse it.

How the picture changes by context

In a consumer product like Kamini Home's, paid social and paid search dominate early because consumer purchase decisions are often impulsive and immediate, and earned channels — reviews, unboxing videos, word of mouth among friends who share similar taste — become powerful once volume is high enough to generate a visible base of organic advocates; owned channels center on email, SMS, and increasingly a branded app, aimed at driving the repeat purchases that determine whether the original paid acquisition cost was ever worth paying. In a B2B product, the picture inverts in emphasis even though the same three families apply: consider Kunal Cloud Systems, a Chennai-based workflow-automation vendor selling to mid-market manufacturers, where earned channels — analyst mentions, customer case studies, a sales rep's own professional reputation, conference talks — carry disproportionate weight because B2B buyers are risk-averse with budgets they must justify internally and trust signals from peers matter more than an advertisement ever will; owned channels there mean a content library, webinars, and a well-run LinkedIn presence aimed at staying visible through a purchase cycle that can run six to eighteen months; and paid channels, while present, are usually aimed not at direct conversion but at retargeting known accounts already in a sales pipeline, since B2B search volume for a niche category is often too thin to buy meaningful scale. In a marketplace product, the triangle gets applied twice, once for each side of the market — a ride-hailing or classifieds marketplace might spend paid budget acquiring riders or buyers while relying almost entirely on referral and earned mechanisms to acquire the supply side, drivers or sellers, because supply-side participants trust other participants' testimony about earnings far more than an advertisement promising them. Company stage matters as much as product category: an early-stage company with no organic search authority, no email list, and no reputation has little choice but to lean on paid to learn what messaging and audience work at all, treating that early paid spend partly as a research cost rather than a pure acquisition cost, while a large, established company with years of accumulated content, search rankings, and brand reputation can often let owned and earned channels carry a rising share of volume, redirecting paid budget toward defending market share and launching genuinely new products rather than sustaining the base business.

Common mistakes

The first common mistake is treating "marketing budget" as one undifferentiated pool and asking only "how much" rather than "which channel." The symptom an outside observer would see is a company whose entire growth conversation is a single number — this month's ad spend — with no separate line for content, email, or public relations; the underlying misunderstanding is believing more money is always the lever, when the actual constraint is often channel maturity or audience exhaustion rather than budget. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask what the company's CAC trend has looked like over the last six months at rising spend: a rising CAC trend while spend rises is the auction telling the company it has already captured the cheap customers.

The second common mistake is confusing an owned channel's low marginal cost with a fast payoff, and abandoning owned-channel investment — an email program, a blog, a community — after eight or ten weeks because it "isn't working" compared to paid. The symptom is a graveyard of half-built company blogs and dormant email sequences; the underlying misunderstanding is applying a paid-channel timeline, days to weeks, to a channel that compounds over quarters. The cheapest diagnostic is simply asking, before funding an owned-channel initiative, what the expected time-to-payoff is and whether the team has committed to funding it through that entire horizon, not just through the first disappointing month.

The third common mistake is trying to manufacture earned media through inauthentic means — fake reviews, paid-for "organic-looking" influencer posts without disclosure, manufactured controversy — because earned reach is the hardest of the three to generate honestly and the temptation to shortcut it is strong. The symptom is a spike in mentions that does not translate into retained customers, or worse, a platform or regulatory penalty; the underlying misunderstanding is treating earned media as a channel that can be bought quietly rather than a channel that must be genuinely invited. The cheapest diagnostic is asking whether the company would be comfortable disclosing exactly how each piece of "earned" coverage was obtained.

The fourth common mistake, the one closest to Rhea's own board-room pressure, is assuming a channel's past growth rate will continue linearly as spend scales, ignoring that most paid auctions and even most owned-audience growth curves are concave, not linear. The symptom is a growth plan built entirely on multiplying last month's cost-per-result by a bigger number; the underlying misunderstanding is treating a channel's early efficiency as its steady-state efficiency. The cheapest diagnostic is a small, deliberate spend increase — 20% rather than 100% — measured before committing to the full scale-up, precisely to observe where the cost curve bends.

What good looks like

Two years after Rhea's board meeting, a comparable decision at a different company, Kunal Cloud Systems, was handled the way this framework recommends. Facing pressure to hit an ambitious pipeline target, Kunal's head of marketing resisted the instinct to simply double the paid LinkedIn budget and instead built a nine-month plan that funded three things in parallel from the start: a modestly scaled paid-retargeting budget aimed only at accounts already engaged with sales, a genuinely useful owned content library of implementation guides that ranked in search results customers were already typing, and a deliberate earned-media push built on getting three existing customers to speak publicly about measurable results, which then became the centerpiece of both the owned content and the paid retargeting creative. The three channels were sequenced, not competing for the same budget line, and each fed the others — the case studies became landing pages, the landing pages became ad creative, and the ad creative drove traffic back to a content library built to convert on its own. Nine months later, paid delivered exactly what it was suited for, fast and controllable volume during the ramp, while owned and earned had matured enough to be carrying a majority of new pipeline, at a fraction of paid's cost per lead — precisely the balance a channel strategy is meant to produce, and precisely the balance Kamini Home was nine months away from itself.

Closing

Rhea's proposal to the board did not ask for less money; it asked for the same total marketing budget, split three ways instead of one. She kept paid spend roughly flat rather than doubling it, protecting it from the cost curve she had modelled, and redirected the incremental capital toward two hires and one system: a lifecycle-marketing associate to finally activate the email list and turn Kamini Home's dormant Instagram following into a genuine content engine, and a modest budget for a structured post-purchase review and referral program designed to convert Kamini Home's already-strong product satisfaction into visible, citable earned reach. The board approved a version of the plan with a shorter runway than Rhea wanted — six months rather than nine to show owned and earned contributing meaningfully — but approved it nonetheless, persuaded less by the framework's vocabulary than by the arithmetic underneath it: a scenario in which the company's only lever was a channel that would turn unprofitable at the very revenue level the board was asking for. What Rhea took from the episode, and what she flagged as her own next area to study, was how thin her attribution model still was — she could see which channel a customer's first click came from, but not how the three channels were interacting to produce it, and she suspected, correctly, that resolving that would require learning how marketing funnels actually connect awareness to consideration to purchase, one layer beneath the channel question itself. Two questions worth sitting with, for any reader facing a version of Rhea's decision: if your own paid channel's cost curve bent the way Kamini Home's did, would your current reporting even show you the bend before it became a loss — and which of your owned or earned channels, if you funded it patiently for two full quarters rather than two months, might already be capable of carrying real volume?

Prasaar Customs Cloud: The Channel Mix at Thoothukudi

Thoothukudi, Tamil Nadu — Sunday, 8 February 2026

1. The night before

The gantry cranes at V.O. Chidambaranar Port were still lit at half past ten, and from the Prasaar Customs Cloud office on Palayamkottai Road, Revathi Alagappan could hear trailers queueing for the freight stations north of the harbour. The board pre-read was open on her laptop: eleven slides, nine finished. The tenth, titled “FY2026-27 channel mix”, held one sentence she had typed and deleted four times.

At nine the next morning she would put a recommendation to Deepan Valliappan, the co-founder and chief executive, and, over video from Mumbai, to the Vaanam Growth Capital partner holding the board seat. She had ₹360.00 lakh of go-to-market budget for the year from 1 April 2026, up from ₹240.00 lakh in the twelve months just closed. The board had a number of its own: ₹36.00 crore of annual recurring revenue by 31 March 2027, against a forecast ₹27.00 crore this financial year.

Three weeks of arithmetic had brought her somewhere uncomfortable. She could defend three very different mixes of paid, owned and earned. None reached ₹36.00 crore. The gap between her best plan and the board minutes was ₹371.90 lakh, and the honest version of slide ten said so. She did not know whether Monday was a decision about channels at all, or about what to tell the board.

2. How Prasaar got here

Prasaar Customs Cloud was founded in 2017 by Deepan Valliappan, who had spent nine years as a customs house agent in his family's firm at Thoothukudi. The first product was unglamorous: a filing assistant that validated a shipping bill against tariff headings and pushed it to ICEGATE without the three rounds of rejection a junior clerk's typing produced. It sold slowly, to agents along the coast who paid ₹7,500 a quarter and told each other about it at the association tea stall.

By 2020 Prasaar had added a freight station module, and by 2022 a shipper dashboard. The product now spanned four customer types of wildly different sizes, a fact that would matter. Exhibit 1 sets out the base at 31 December 2025.

One decision still binds the company. In March 2023, to win Nauka Terminal Services — a freight station operator with yards at Thoothukudi and Chennai, and Prasaar's first large logo at ₹1.20 crore over three years — Deepan agreed to two clauses: a most-favoured-customer term on pricing, and an undertaking, uncontroversial then, that Prasaar would appoint no reseller or implementation partner inside the V.O. Chidambaranar Port customs zone without Nauka's written consent. Prasaar had no partners and no intention of any. It runs to 31 March 2027. Tatpar Trade Networks, the Tirunelveli documentation firm with which Prasaar piloted a partner programme in 2025, works that zone every day.

3. The industry around the yard gate

India's export-import paperwork sits on public rails: ICEGATE carries the filings, the CBIC sets procedure, the DGFT tracks licences, and since the National Logistics Policy of 2022 the Unified Logistics Interface Platform has pulled document flows together. Every change in that machinery — a tariff notification, a revision to the e-way bill rules, a GST format that shifts under an exporter's feet — produces a week of confusion at every yard gate, and a spike of traffic to whoever explains it first.

The competitive field is crowded and quiet. Phailav Trade Systems, out of Navi Mumbai, sells a broader suite into the JNPA and Mundra corridors and undercuts Prasaar wherever the two meet. Larger groups — Allcargo, CONCOR, the terminal operators at Adani Ports and DP World's Indian facilities — increasingly build their own systems, capping how far upmarket a Thoothukudi company can go. Tamil Nadu's software reputation, built by Zoho and Freshworks, helps Prasaar hire; it does nothing for it in Kandla.

Two forces sit under the plan. Vizhinjam's ramp-up and the Colombo diversions have made cargo routing less predictable. And the DPDP Act has landed on a database of importer records and consignee addresses: compliance is consuming one and a half engineers through June 2026 — engineers not building the partner-facing API a reseller motion needs. Abroad, Sahil Marine Logistics LLC, a forwarder at Jebel Ali, took a fourteen-seat licence in 2024 and wants a Gulf deployment; it is Prasaar's only reference outside India, worth more as reference than revenue.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The debate began with a number that flattered everybody: in April 2025 Prasaar switched on last-touch attribution, crediting whichever source last touched an opportunity before qualification. Exhibit 2 is the twelve months to 31 December 2025 read that way — 1,500 qualified opportunities, 325 wins at a blended win rate of 21.7 per cent, ₹240.00 lakh of spend and ₹432.40 lakh of new annual recurring revenue.

Read naively, the story is simple. Paid — search, trade portals, the booth programme at port conclaves — absorbed ₹160.00 lakh of the ₹240.00 lakh envelope, or 66.7 per cent, and returned 96 of the 325 wins, 29.5 per cent. Earned — associations and the WhatsApp groups where agents warn each other about rejected bills — cost ₹20.00 lakh and returned 100 wins, at ₹0.20 lakh a win against paid's ₹1.67 lakh. By August that was policy, and Dinakar Palaniappan's content team was told to double its output.

Then value per win arrived. Paid's 96 wins carried ₹194.40 lakh of ARR, a shade over ₹2.00 lakh each: the fairs and listings were where the freight station operators and larger forwarders were. Earned's 100 wins carried ₹87.10 lakh, ₹0.87 lakh each; word of mouth travels fastest among the smallest agents, who pay least. Paid took 45.0 per cent of new ARR on 66.7 per cent of spend; earned 20.1 per cent on 8.3 per cent. The gap was real, and less than half as wide as the win counts implied.

Then attribution came apart. In December, Rukmani Arunachalam rebuilt the model from raw touch logs and a 140-response survey. Exhibit 4 sets three readings of the same 325 wins side by side. Under first-touch, paid rises from 96 wins to 174 and its cost per win falls to ₹0.92 lakh, against the ₹1.67 lakh on which the August policy was built; under multi-touch it sits at 138 wins and ₹1.16 lakh. What the logs showed was that 71 per cent of the opportunities credited to earned carried a prior paid touch: the association secretary who recommended Prasaar had first met it at a session Prasaar paid ₹3.40 lakh to host.

Exhibit 5 added a third axis. Earned-sourced accounts were filing on ICEGATE within sixty days at 88 per cent against 58 per cent for paid-sourced ones, and raised 1.9 tickets a month against 4.8; on the 2024 cohort, gross churn at twelve months was 7 per cent against 22 per cent. Kalaiselvi Annamalai had said so for a year. But the 2024 cohort was 128 paid-sourced accounts out of 248, or 51.6 per cent, so the churn column describes a smaller and differently weighted population than the win counts beside it.

5. The people in the room

Revathi Alagappan

Head of Product & Go-to-Market · Thoothukudi

Owns Monday's recommendation. Says Prasaar spent a year optimising a number three models dispute.

Not saying: she thinks ₹36.00 crore is unreachable, and cannot decide whether that goes on slide ten.

Deepan Valliappan

Co-founder & CEO · Thoothukudi

Wants the number hit; believes the fairs are where Prasaar is taken seriously. Signed the Nauka clauses.

Not saying: two acquisition approaches have come in, and he reads FY27 as the price of independence.

Karthik Somasundaram

VP Enterprise Sales · Tirunelveli

Paid-led. Every freight station logo came from a booth, a listing or outbound; the pilot converts faster than his team.

Not saying: his variable pay rides on new-logo ARR, which no owned or earned programme credits him.

Kalaiselvi Annamalai

Head of Implementation & Success · Ramanathapuram

Argues earned growth is an output of implementation quality, not a channel to be funded.

Not saying: she is nine people short, and Plan C is the only Monday in which she gets them.

Dinakar Palaniappan

Head of Content & Community · Thoothukudi

Runs owned: the tariff bulletin, the ICEGATE webinar, the referral prompt. Wants two writers before the season.

Not saying: bulletin subscriptions have been flat since October, and he has not circulated the chart.

Rukmani Arunachalam

Staff Data Scientist · Bengaluru

Built Exhibit 4 and will not name a preferred model: the choice, she says, is commercial, dressed as technical.

Not saying: the survey sample is too small for the weight put on it; she said so once, unanswered.

Devaraj Karuppiah

Chief Financial Officer · Thoothukudi

Will not sign a plan whose blended cost per win rises above last year's ₹0.74 lakh. Wants the fairs line cut.

Not saying: the FY27 milestone carries a ratchet, and he has not shared what missing it costs the founders.

Nadia Mansour

Group Operations Director, Sahil Marine Logistics LLC · Jebel Ali

Wants a Gulf deployment by October 2026, and will introduce two Jebel Ali forwarders if so.

Not saying: her group is evaluating Phailav Trade Systems in parallel, on a timetable Prasaar does not know.

That lasted four minutes, until she thought what a reset number does to a term sheet she had never been shown.

Outside, a trailer took the turn to the yard gate too fast. The bulletin's flat subscriber chart was still open in another tab; she had not asked Dinakar about it, and was fairly sure he was waiting to be asked. The pre-read was due in under eight hours, and slide ten was empty again.

Setu Shiksha Cloud: Choosing a Channel Mix Before the Signing Season

Mangaluru, Karnataka — Friday, 14 November 2025

1. The decision on Tanvi's desk

Tanvi Poojary, Head of Growth and GTM at Setu Shiksha Cloud, had a half-built spreadsheet open and nineteen days to finish it. From the third-floor office off Kadri she could see the Netravati flowing toward the port — a fitting view for a company named for a bridge. On 5 December, Setu's board would approve the go-to-market budget for the stretch to 31 March 2026, the last date a new customer could be signed, onboarded and billing before the April renewal window closed. The board had set one hard number: at least 60 net-new schools live by then, carrying Setu's base past 310 schools and revenue past ₹12.40 crore — the run-rate Harshad Shenoy, co-founder and CEO, wanted for the Series A talks in April.

Tanvi had ₹90 lakh to spend across paid, owned and earned, and a dashboard, built by Elena Novak in Toronto, showing exactly what each had cost and returned. The arithmetic was not the hard part. Three different ways of spending ₹90 lakh all cleared the board's number on paper, and Tanvi knew a spreadsheet total was not the same as a signed, trusting customer.

2. Setu Shiksha Cloud

Harshad Shenoy founded Setu Shiksha Cloud in 2019 after eleven years at Infosys, when his son's school in Mangaluru spent three days each term reconciling fee ledgers by hand. Setu sells a cloud fee-management and light school-ERP suite: fee collection over UPI and Razorpay, a parent app, attendance and report cards, and an admissions module tuned to the paperwork private K-12 chains file under state boards and the RTE Act. The company bootstrapped through 2022, raised a ₹3.5 crore seed round from a Bengaluru angel syndicate, and spent two years building density along the coastal Karnataka–Kerala belt — Mangaluru, Udupi, Kasaragod — before pushing into Bengaluru and Kochi.

As of 14 November 2025, Setu serves 250 schools at an average contract value of ₹4.00 lakh, a run-rate of ₹1,000.00 lakh, or ₹10.00 crore. Teachmint and Fedena sell comparable ERP suites nationally; Entab is entrenched with CBSE chains in the north. Jodo and the school-lending NBFC Varthana sit in the same fee-side conversations. Every contract touches the DPDP Act, since the product holds student and parent data.

3. The situation

Setu earns leads three ways. Paid is Google and Meta campaigns, fair booths, and outbound from a six-person sales pod — including Nakul Kamath, Enterprise Sales Lead, who works the Gulf from Dubai. Owned is a two-person content and SEO effort: compliance explainers, trustee webinars, in-app referral prompts. Earned is word of mouth — principals recommending Setu at PTA meetings and conferences, and unpaid press.

Exhibit 1 shows how each performed between April and September 2025. Paid demo requests closed at 20 of 500, a 4.0 per cent conversion rate, for ₹60 lakh — a CAC of ₹3.00 lakh per school. Owned converted 18 of 300 (6.0 per cent) for ₹9 lakh, or ₹0.50 lakh per school. Earned converted 15 of 150 (10.0 per cent) for ₹6 lakh, the cheapest at ₹0.40 lakh per school. Together the three added 53 schools, taking Setu from 197 in March to the current 250.

Two facts complicate a simple "spend more on the cheap channels" instinct. Nakul's sales-ops model shows paid's cost does not hold as spend rises: the first ₹60 lakh buys schools at ₹3.00 lakh each, but every rupee beyond that buys leads outside the coastal belt's playbook at roughly ₹5.00 lakh, since the pod cannot add capacity mid-cycle. Owned and earned are capacity-bound, not budget-bound: the content team's ceiling for two quarters is about 500 demo requests — at 6.0 per cent conversion, 30 schools, costing ₹15 lakh. Amoolya Shetty, Customer Success Lead in Singapore, runs the promoter survey behind earned: her read puts its ceiling at roughly 25 schools, since referral only draws from principals who already trust Setu.

Two more inputs shaped the debate. Amoolya's cohort data shows first-term activation averaging 84 per cent among earned-sourced schools against 61 per cent among paid-sourced ones. In Dubai, Nakul has Evergreen International School Group — a 14-campus CBSE chain across Dubai and Sharjah — in late-stage evaluation, sourced through paid outbound. It sits outside the ₹90 lakh envelope and Exhibit 2 below, since it is a single negotiation and Setu has no other Gulf reference yet. Jonas Reiter, the designer in Berlin, worries the same principals who see Setu's ads are the ones it wants writing referrals.

4. The people

Owns the recommendation. Wants a mix defensible on cost, timing and credibility — not just the biggest number.

Harshad Shenoy

Owns the promoter survey and activation data. Wants earned scaled carefully, not stretched past the trust it is built on.

Nakul Kamath

6. The options

Option A — Lean into paid

Upside: Paid's 45-day cycle makes its 67 schools the most likely to be signed and billing before 31 March, echoing the outbound motion already working on Evergreen.

Cost: Highest blended CAC, ₹1.34 lakh per school, from the expensive incremental tier; lower activation (61 vs 84 per cent); and, per Jonas, ad fatigue risk among the trustees Setu needs for referrals.

Option B — Owned and earned first

Upside: The largest outcome of the three — 76 schools, ₹304.00 lakh ARR added, at a low CAC of ₹1.18 lakh per school — by pushing owned and earned to their 30- and 25-school ceilings.

Cost: Owned and earned's 90- and 60-day cycles mean much of this pipeline risks closing after 31 March. Pushing past a trust-built ceiling also risks diluting the credibility that makes earned cheap.

Option C — Hold paid, fill the ceilings, bank the rest

Upside: Captures the full owned and earned ceilings — the cheapest, most credible, already-in-motion volume — while capping paid at its sustainable rate. CAC of ₹1.13 lakh per school, with ₹5 lakh held in reserve.

Cost: Fewer schools than B (75 vs 76), leaning more on owned and earned reaching their ceilings on schedule.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, what does each channel trade between control, cost and credibility — and why might that matter more here than the raw CAC figures alone?
  2. Exhibit 2 shows Option B signs the most schools (76), while Option C has the lowest blended CAC. Why might Tanvi still hesitate to recommend Option B?
  3. What does the gap in average sales cycle (Exhibit 1, Exhibit 3) imply about which option most reliably hits 31 March — and does clearing the board's 60-school bar actually settle the question?
  4. If you were Tanvi, how would you use Amoolya's activation data and Nakul's Evergreen pipeline to make the case to Harshad on 5 December?

8. A note for the learner

This topic asks what each channel trades between control, cost and credibility. Paid buys control over timing at the highest cost and weakest trust. Owned is cheap but bound by team capacity. Earned is cheapest and most credible, but cannot be manufactured on demand; it is bounded by the goodwill of the existing base, and pushing past that ceiling risks corroding the trust that makes it work.

A well-reasoned answer does not stop at Exhibit 2's totals, since all three options clear the board's 60-school bar. It has to reason about which schools close in time. The defensible path is Option C: fill owned and earned to their genuine ceilings, hold paid at its proven ₹3.00 lakh rate instead of the expensive tier, and keep ₹5 lakh in reserve to top up whichever channel underperforms. It is not the single largest number on the page, but the mix least dependent on one assumption holding — incremental paid CAC staying at ₹5.00 lakh, or every late owned lead closing in time.

Option A is defensible too, if timeline certainty outweighs the activation and credibility cost, argued explicitly. Option B is the right multi-year bet in a trust-driven market, but the weakest choice against this deadline, since it depends on cycle times the calendar does not allow. The case really tests the difference between a channel that is cheap and one that is ready in time.
