Channels: Paid, Owned, Earned

Near-expert depth. The three families are not three budget lines. They are three different cost curves, three different time constants, and — in the case of earned — not a channel at all but a multiplier on the other two. This page argues that case, works the arithmetic, and leaves the parts the field has not settled visibly unsettled.

1. Two rooms, five weeks apart

On the morning of 9 February 2026, Ira Deshmukh took a printout into a windowless room on the second floor of Mandakini Diagnostics Systems in Pune and put a single slide on the table. Mandakini built a benchtop haematology analyser — a five-part differential machine that sits in a hospital laboratory and counts blood cells — paired with a cloud quality-control service that tracks calibration drift across every installed instrument. The device sold for ₹6.8 lakh; the software attached at ₹14,000 a month. In the financial year closing in March, Mandakini had placed 96 instruments. The board wanted 220 in FY27. Ira, who had run product for three years and had inherited the commercial function in October, had spent a fortnight building the number she now had to defend: Mandakini's fully-loaded commercial cost — eleven field representatives, two application specialists, trade-show presence, collateral, the demo fleet — came to ₹2.9 crore, which against 96 placements meant a customer acquisition cost of ₹3.02 lakh per instrument. Over three years each placement returned ₹2.58 lakh of gross profit on the hardware and ₹4.13 lakh on the software subscription: ₹6.71 lakh in all, a ratio of 2.2 to one. The board's instruction had been phrased helpfully. Build a modern channel mix. You are too dependent on feet on the street. Ira's slide said that the total monthly search volume in India for every term a laboratory head might type when shopping for an analyser of this class was approximately 480 — and that if Mandakini won every one of those searches, converted three per cent to a qualified lead and nine per cent of those leads to a placement, paid search would deliver about 1.3 instruments a month. The board wanted 124 additional placements. The auction the board was asking her to buy did not exist.

Five weeks later and 840 kilometres south, Sanjay Raghavan had the opposite problem. Madhav Intelligence, which he had co-founded in Bengaluru in 2022, sold an AI-native support-automation product: a system that read a company's help centre, ticket history and product documentation and then resolved inbound customer queries end to end. Revenue stood at ₹41 crore of annual recurring revenue across roughly 3,100 paying workspaces, split between a self-serve tier averaging ₹1.1 lakh a year and a mid-market motion averaging ₹9.4 lakh. Madhav spent ₹1.35 crore a quarter on paid acquisition, mostly search and a programmatic retargeting layer, and the dashboard reported a return on ad spend of 4.1 times. In January Sanjay had authorised something most companies at his stage never authorise: a genuine geographic holdout, in which paid spend was switched off entirely in four Indian metros and two South-East Asian markets for nine weeks while it ran normally in six matched control geographies. The result landed on 13 March. Measured incrementally — signups that would not have happened otherwise — the return was 1.6 times, not 4.1. Roughly thirty-four per cent of what the dashboard called a paid conversion came from people typing the word "Madhav" into a search box, seeing the company's own advertisement above its own organic listing, and clicking the advertisement. Sanjay had, on the most conservative reading, been paying a search engine several crore a year to be introduced to people who already knew his company's name.

Both executives were about to make a channel decision, and both were about to discover that the familiar three-part taxonomy — paid, owned, earned — was necessary but nowhere near sufficient for the decision in front of them. Ira's problem was that one of the three families had no purchasable inventory in her market at all. Sanjay's problem was that his measurement system could not tell him which family a customer had actually come from, and therefore his allocation had been drifting for two years toward whichever family produced the cleanest dashboard. The argument of this page is that both problems have the same root: practitioners treat paid, owned and earned as three parallel places to put money, when in fact they are three objects of different kinds — a rented flow, a depreciating asset, and a multiplier — and that almost every serious channel mistake is a category error about which of those three kinds you are handling.

2. The idea, and the five schools that disagree about it

Start with a definition tight enough to argue with. A channel is a route by which a company's message or product reaches a prospective customer. The paid–owned–earned taxonomy sorts routes by the answer to two questions asked together: who holds the right to place the message, and what was surrendered to obtain that right. In a paid channel the right is rented from a third party for money, per exposure or per period, and lapses the instant payment stops. In an owned channel the right is held by the company itself — its site, its application surface, its consented email and messaging list, its documentation, its retail counter, its installed base — acquired by building rather than renting, and retained until it is allowed to decay. In an earned channel the right is held by a third party who exercises it in the company's favour without payment: a journalist, a clinician, a developer on a forum, a customer telling a colleague, or — increasingly — a language model citing the company in an answer.

The vocabulary is younger than the practice. The underlying distinction is the old agency split between advertising, which bought space, and public relations, which did not, a division formalised in the trade well before the war and given its cynical modern shape in the 1920s by publicists who understood that a newspaper's endorsement carried weight precisely because it could not be purchased openly. Through the post-war decades agencies talked instead of "above the line" and "below the line" — a distinction about commission structure, not about control. What changed in the mid-1990s was the corporate website: for the first time a company held a substantial standing media property that it neither rented nor earned, and the existing vocabulary had no slot for it. The three-part phrasing as it is used today was popularised in a 2009 research note out of Forrester by Sean Corcoran, and elaborated across 2010 and 2011 in the advertising trade press as brands began arguing internally about whether a Facebook page was a media buy, a website, or a public-relations exercise. In 2014 Gini Dietrich added a fourth term — shared — producing the PESO model still taught in communications programmes, on the argument that social platforms are neither owned nor earned but a third thing: a distribution surface a company occupies at a landlord's discretion. Anyone who has watched an organic reach algorithm change overnight will recognise the force of that amendment.

Five schools now hold genuinely different positions, and it is worth stating the proposition each would and would not sign, because a practitioner who cannot locate a colleague's argument in this map will mistake a philosophical disagreement for an analytical error.

The taxonomists hold that the three families differ in kind and must be budgeted separately with different horizons and different success criteria. They will sign: an owned audience is a balance-sheet item that should be valued, depreciated and defended like any other asset. They will not sign: earned reach can be forecast to a quarterly number. Their evidence is the repeated observation that companies which fund only what pays back inside a quarter arrive at year five with no asset at all.

The incrementalists — the econometric and experimentation tradition that now dominates large performance organisations — hold that the taxonomy is a narrative overlay that conceals substitution between channels, and that the only defensible classification is measured incremental contribution per marginal rupee. They will sign: a geographic holdout beats every attribution model ever built. They will not sign: owned media is nearly free, on the grounds that an owned channel which merely re-captures demand that paid or earned created has no incremental value whatever, however cheap its marginal send. Their evidence is the now-large body of holdout results, including Sanjay's, in which last-click return exceeds measured incremental return by factors of two to three.

The mental-availability school, associated with the Ehrenberg-Bass tradition and, in its budgeting form, with Les Binet and Peter Field's long-and-short work, holds that the meaningful split is not paid versus earned but long-term brand building versus short-term activation, in roughly a sixty-forty ratio of spend, and that credibility is a far weaker force than sheer reach and memorability. They will sign: most of what companies proudly classify as direct, organic and word of mouth is paid reach from eighteen months ago, arriving late. They will not sign: word of mouth is a channel you can invest in directly.

The distribution-is-product school, native to product-led growth and to network-effects thinking, holds that channels are features: that the highest-leverage channel work happens inside the product — sharing, invitations, integration marketplaces, embedded surfaces, marketplace supply — and that marketing channels are a tax you pay for not having built distribution into the artefact. They will sign: the most valuable channel decision most companies make is a roadmap decision. They will not sign: you can buy a durable channel advantage.

The permission school is the newest and, in India, the most legally grounded. It holds that in a world of deprecated third-party identifiers, platform walled gardens, and statutory consent regimes — the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023, the telecom regulator's distributed-ledger registration requirement for commercial messaging — the only durable asset is a consented, identity-resolved, reachable relationship, and that paid and earned are both merely ways of filling that reservoir. They will sign: reachable consented contacts, not revenue, is the leading indicator of a consumer company's next two years. They will not sign: reach without permission compounds.

Held together, the five schools agree on almost nothing except this: whatever else the three families are, they are not interchangeable places to put the same rupee.

3. Mechanics in depth: three objects, three mathematics

Expert practice begins by refusing the single word "channel" and asking, for each route, what kind of object it is. A paid channel is a flow purchased at a price that rises with quantity. An owned channel is a stock that accrues, depreciates and requires maintenance. Earned is a multiplier applied to whatever the other two deliver. Each has its own arithmetic, and the arithmetic is where competent practitioners separate from expert ones.

Paid: the elasticity, not the average

Nearly every company quotes a single customer acquisition cost. That number is a point on a curve, and the curve's shape matters more than the point. The standard empirical form, used in marketing-mix modelling since the 1970s and still the workhorse, is a constant-elasticity response: customers Q = a · Sb, where S is spend and b, the elasticity, lies between zero and one. Average cost per customer is S/Q. Marginal cost — what the next customer costs — follows by differentiation, and the result is compact enough to memorise and far too rarely used:

Marginal CAC = Average CAC ÷ elasticity. If a channel's spend elasticity is 0.5, the next customer costs twice the average. At 0.7, 1.43 times. At 0.35, nearly three times. The number a growth team quotes is almost never the number that governs its next decision.

Sanjay's holdout let Madhav fit b honestly, because a holdout gives you two points on the curve rather than one. Fitted across the six treatment geographies, self-serve paid elasticity came out at 0.52. Average paid CAC on the self-serve tier was ₹34,000. Marginal CAC was therefore about ₹65,400 — against a self-serve gross profit of roughly ₹79,000 over an expected 2.3-year life at 82 per cent gross margin. The channel was not unprofitable at the margin. It was, however, producing a payback on the marginal customer of eleven months rather than the six months the board's model assumed, and every additional crore of quarterly spend would push it further. The table below shows why arguing about average CAC is nearly always arguing about the wrong quantity.

Two second-order effects sit underneath this and are routinely left implicit. The first is carryover, or adstock: an exposure today produces conversions for several weeks afterward, conventionally modelled as a geometric decay with weekly retention λ, so that the total effect of a burst is 1/(1−λ) times its same-week effect. Madhav's fitted λ was 0.45, implying a long-run multiplier of 1.82. A four-week test window would therefore have understated paid's true contribution by close to a third — which is exactly the error made by teams that switch spend off for a fortnight, see little change, and conclude paid does nothing. The second is test power, which decides whether a holdout can answer the question at all. Madhav's control geographies averaged 1,240 weekly signups with a standard deviation of 145. To detect a ten per cent lift at eighty per cent power and conventional significance requires roughly 2(1.96+0.84)²σ²/δ² ≈ 22 geo-weeks per arm; with six geographies per arm that is a four-week minimum, and Sanjay ran nine. Most holdouts that "find nothing" were never powered to find anything, and reporting a null from an underpowered test as evidence of no effect is one of the more expensive statistical sins committed in growth teams.

Owned: an asset with maintenance, not a free channel

The standard teaching — owned media is front-loaded rather than free — is true and insufficient. The expert treatment values an owned channel the way one values any asset: as the discounted stream of contribution it throws off, net of the cost of keeping it alive, at a discount rate that includes its decay.

Take a real case. Mitravinda Bazaar, a Jaipur marketplace for handloom and handicraft goods that will return in section eight, held 310,000 email-consented buyers, of whom 41 per cent — about 127,000 — had opened anything in ninety days. A campaign send to that reachable list opened at 24 per cent; nine per cent of openers clicked; 3.1 per cent of the resulting 2,743 sessions converted, at an average order value of ₹2,240 and a 31 per cent gross margin. That is 85 orders and ₹59,024 of gross profit per send. At four sends a month the list produced ₹2.36 lakh monthly, or ₹28.3 lakh a year. Applying a 22 per cent annual list decay and a 16 per cent discount rate, the perpetuity value is 28.3 ÷ 0.38 ≈ ₹74.5 lakh. Against that sits the lifecycle function that keeps the list alive: one associate, creative, the messaging platform, deliverability work — ₹6.4 lakh a year, which capitalised at 16 per cent is ₹40 lakh. The list was an asset worth roughly ₹34.5 lakh net.

That is a positive number, and it is a much smaller positive number than anyone at Mitravinda expected. The general point matters more than the specific one: an owned channel is an asset only when the contribution it throws off exceeds the cost of maintaining it, and that is not automatic. A company blog that requires two writers and produces four hundred sessions a month is not a cheap channel; it is a loss-making subsidiary with a content calendar. The discipline is to run the same discounted calculation on every owned property annually and be willing to shut one down — an act almost no marketing organisation performs voluntarily, because owned properties accumulate sentimental and political ownership faster than they accumulate traffic.

Earned: a multiplier, with a formal treatment

The single most useful reframing available to a practitioner is this: earned reach is not a third column in the budget. It is a reproduction number applied to the customers the other two families deliver. Borrow the branching-process arithmetic from epidemiology. Let k be the expected number of additional customers generated, directly or indirectly, by each acquired customer through unpaid transmission — a referral, a recommendation in a professional group, a review that converts a stranger. Then each directly acquired customer ultimately yields 1/(1−k) customers in total, and the effective acquisition cost of the whole cohort is the nominal cost multiplied by (1−k).

The consequence for budgeting is sharp. If earned is a multiplier rather than a channel, then the question "how much should we spend on earned?" is malformed. The well-formed questions are: what determines k in this business, is it something marketing can move, and if not, who owns the thing that does? In almost every case the answer to the second question is no. k is set by whether a customer has something worth saying — a result they can quote, a defect they did not encounter, a moment of relief. Marketing can remove friction from transmission, by asking for the review at the right moment or by making the referral a single tap. It cannot manufacture the reason to tell.

4. When the framework applies, stated as claims you can test

A framework that always applies explains nothing. Four conditions decide whether the paid–owned–earned lens is doing work in a given business, and each can be turned into a test that a competent analyst could run in a week.

Claim one: the families have materially different elasticities in this business. Test: fit each family's response separately and check whether the elasticities differ by more than about 0.2. Where they do not — and there are such businesses, typically commoditised retail categories where everything is price-driven — the taxonomy adds vocabulary without adding decisions, and the team should be running a single cost-per-order optimisation across all routes. For Madhav the difference was stark: paid at 0.52, documentation-driven organic at something close to 0.9 over the range tested, meaning the owned family had not begun to saturate. For Mandakini, paid elasticity was effectively irrelevant because the intercept was so low.

Claim two: the purchase has a credibility bottleneck. Test: does the buying decision require the buyer to be convinced of something an interested party cannot credibly assert? For an analyser that will generate clinical results on which patient treatment depends, the answer is emphatically yes — no advertisement can establish that a machine's differential counts agree with the reference method at a particular hospital's patient mix. For Madhav's self-serve tier, largely no: a support manager can run a fourteen-day trial and see for herself, which is why product experience substitutes for credibility in product-led motions and why earned matters less there than practitioners expect.

Claim three: the company will exist long enough for an owned asset to amortise. Test: compare the owned channel's modelled payback against cash runway with a margin. An eighteen-month payback funded from an eleven-month runway is not patience; it is a bet that a fundraise will happen, and it should be argued as such. This is the single most common place where the standard advice — balance the three, be patient with owned — is wrong for a specific company. A pre-Series-A business with nine months of cash should be almost entirely in paid and founder-led earned, not because owned is bad but because it cannot collect on it.

Claim four: purchasable attention exists at meaningful scale. Test: estimate the total addressable inventory — search volume, qualified audience size on the relevant platforms, list rental universe — and compute the maximum customers obtainable at one hundred per cent share of voice. Ira's 1.3 instruments a month is that calculation, and it is the calculation almost nobody performs before writing a paid strategy. In markets whose buyers number in the hundreds, paid media is not a channel; it is at best an air-cover expense that makes a field representative's call slightly warmer.

There is a fifth situation in which the framework is not merely inapplicable but actively misleading, and it deserves naming. When distribution is structurally intermediated — an app store, a modern-trade retail shelf, an original-equipment preload, a group purchasing organisation, a systems-integrator partner, an insurance broker — the route is neither paid nor owned nor earned. It is negotiated: obtained through a commercial agreement with terms, exclusivity, margin splits and renewal risk. Calling a retail shelf "paid" because you paid slotting fees misses that what you actually bought was a contract with a counterparty whose interests will diverge from yours, and whose renewal decision will not be made on your cost-per-acquisition. Several serious practitioners argue for a fourth family on exactly these grounds, and in businesses where negotiated distribution carries most of the volume — consumer packaged goods, medical devices, most hardware — the three-part model describes perhaps a third of what matters.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

Multi-product companies face a commons problem in owned media. The email list, the homepage, the in-product notification slot and the sales team's attention are shared resources, and every product manager's rational act is to use more of them. The cost is not hypothetical: at Mitravinda, raising promotional send frequency from four to seven a month lifted campaign revenue by 31 per cent for one quarter while raising the monthly unsubscribe-plus-dormancy rate from 1.8 per cent to 4.1 per cent — which, compounded, removes roughly a quarter of the reachable list in a year and destroys far more asset value than the quarter's lift created. Mature companies say they manage this with a "communications calendar". What they actually do, when they do it well, is impose a hard frequency cap, allocate sends as a budget to product lines, and hold one accountable owner for reachable-list size as a standing metric reported next to revenue.

Two-sided businesses must run the taxonomy twice, and the two sides usually need opposite mixes. Supply typically responds to earned — a seller believes another seller's account of monthly earnings far more than a promise — while demand responds to paid. This creates the marketplace cold-start paradox in channel form: the side with the strongest earned potential is the side with nobody to earn from yet. The competent move is to buy the first cohort of supply outright with field operations and incentives, treating the cost as an asset-building expense rather than acquisition, and to switch to earned only once a referenceable cohort exists with numbers worth repeating.

Regulated categories bind earned and owned more tightly than paid. In India, insurance advertising sits under the insurance regulator's advertisement rules, securities and investment communications under the market regulator's requirements, and lending communications under the central bank's fair-practice expectations. A financial services company cannot simply amplify a customer testimonial about returns; an unbranded influencer enthusiasm may create liability the company never authorised. Simultaneously the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 constrains the owned side, requiring purpose-limited, revocable consent for the very messaging list the permission school regards as the core asset, and the telecom regulator's distributed-ledger registration regime means a commercial message that is not properly registered simply does not arrive. The practical effect is counter-intuitive: in regulated categories, paid is often the safest family, because it passes through a compliance review before it ships, while earned is the riskiest because it ships without one.

Hardware plus software puts the earned signal on somebody else's property. Mandakini's reviews, when they exist, live in tender documents, in a laboratory head's WhatsApp group, and in conference abstracts — none of which the company can see, index or respond to. Consumer hardware has the same problem in a more measurable form: the reviews that decide the purchase sit on a marketplace listing the manufacturer does not control, and the manufacturer's own site, its most owned property, is frequently the least consulted surface in the buying journey. Mature hardware companies respond by treating the marketplace listing as an owned channel operationally — staffing it, monitoring question threads, managing the review corpus honestly — while accepting they are tenants.

AI-native products face a live and unresolved shift in what "organic" means. Madhav's own data showed it: in the quarter to March 2026, 22 per cent of self-serve signups who answered the how-did-you-hear question said some variant of "an assistant recommended it". That surface is genuinely novel because it is earned in its mechanics — the company does not control the citation — but owned in its inputs, since what gets cited is documentation, changelogs, comparison pages and structured answers the company wrote. It also collapses part of the traditional owned asset: a search engine result that answers the question inline removes the click that a content library was built to capture. Sanjay's engineering team found that for eleven of Madhav's top twenty informational queries, impressions were flat year on year while sessions had fallen 38 per cent. Whether the correct response is to write more for machines, to abandon the content library and invest in the product surface, or to treat citation share as a new measurable asset class is exactly the kind of question the field has not settled, and any page that tells you otherwise is selling something.

Finally, the organisational seam. Paid usually reports to growth or performance marketing. Owned content reports to product marketing or brand. Community reports to support or developer relations. Public relations reports to communications, often through the chief executive. Referral mechanics live in the product backlog. Nobody owns k. This is the structural reason mature companies drift toward paid regardless of what their strategy documents say: at the quarterly budget meeting, the family with the cleanest dashboard defends its line best, and paid has by far the cleanest dashboard. What well-run companies actually do is not to reorganise — the reorganisation rarely survives — but to force the four functions to present against one shared incrementality-based measurement, ideally an experiment programme owned by a neutral analytics function that none of the four controls.

6. Ten things an expert sees that a competent practitioner does not

The average is a summary of a curve, and the elasticity is the parameter. The tell is a team that quotes a single CAC with no spend level attached and no confidence interval. The obvious reading — the number is the number — is wrong because the number is an average over a spend range the team has not varied deliberately. Ask when the last deliberate spend perturbation happened. If the answer is never, the team does not know its own cost structure; it knows one point on it.

Direct and organic traffic is largely paid media arriving late. The tell is that direct sessions move with the paid budget at a two-to-four-week lag, a correlation visible in almost any company's data once someone thinks to plot it. The obvious reading — direct traffic is our brand strength — is wrong often enough that it should be tested before it is celebrated. Practically: when a holdout switches paid off in a geography, watch whether direct also falls there. At Madhav it fell 19 per cent, which quietly moved several lakh of "free" traffic onto paid's ledger and improved paid's measured incremental return.

Owned channels depreciate, and the depreciation is invisible until it is severe. The tell is a team that reports list size rather than ninety-day-reachable list size, or content-library page count rather than pages that received a session this quarter. The obvious reading — we built it, we have it — is wrong because email lists decay at roughly two to three per cent a month through address churn and disengagement, and content assets decay through ranking changes and now through answer-engine substitution. An owned asset not maintained is not a stable asset; it is a melting one.

Earned reach has a negative tail, and it is the same mechanism. The tell is a company that has modelled how to raise k and has never modelled what happens when k is negative — when the thing people have to say is about an outage, a billing error, or a delivery failure. The obvious reading is that word of mouth is an upside lever. The correct reading is that it is a variance amplifier: the same transmission network that carries delight carries the support-queue regression, and it carries bad news faster, because complaint has higher transmission probability than satisfaction in nearly every measured setting.

Credibility is a property of the relationship between source and buyer, not of the channel. The tell is somebody asserting that earned is more credible than paid without naming an audience. A paid advertisement placed by a national bank in a financial daily may carry more credibility with a conservative buyer than an earned mention by an anonymous enthusiast on a forum. The obvious reading — unpaid means trusted — is wrong because the buyer's inference is about the source's incentives and competence, not about the payment relationship, which the buyer usually cannot observe anyway.

Channel conflict is a pricing problem wearing a marketing costume. The tell is a discounting skirmish between a company's own site and its marketplace listing, or between a direct sales team and a distribution partner chasing the same account. The obvious reading — we need better channel rules — is wrong because the conflict is generated by margin structure, not by rules: as long as the partner earns more by undercutting, rules will be ignored. The fix is almost always a change to price, to assortment differentiation, or to territory economics, and it usually has to come from the commercial leadership, not from marketing.

At fixed budget, reach and frequency trade against each other, and paid platforms optimise toward frequency. The tell is a campaign whose cost per thousand impressions looks stable and whose unique-reach curve has visibly flattened while average frequency climbs past five or six. The obvious reading — the campaign is still efficient — is wrong because the platform is now showing the same advertisement to the same people repeatedly, which is close to the definition of a saturated auction and shows up later as a collapsed elasticity. Check reach, not just cost.

The measurement regime determines the mix more than the strategy does. The tell is a budget that moves materially within a fortnight of an attribution-model change, with no change in the underlying business. The obvious reading is that the new model revealed the truth. The more likely reading is that the organisation funds what it can attribute, and that every attribution change is therefore a covert reallocation. An expert asks, before any model change, which family will lose credit under the new model and whether that family's true contribution has changed at all.

Earned is a lagging indicator of last year's roadmap, not this quarter's marketing. The tell is a growth team being held accountable for a decline in word of mouth that was actually caused by a product regression two quarters earlier, or by a support outsourcing decision. The obvious reading — earned is a marketing outcome — is wrong because the reason to tell is produced by the product and the service, with a lag roughly equal to the customer's usage cycle. When earned falls, the first place to look is the release log and the ticket queue, not the community budget.

The scarce owned asset is consented reachability, not audience size. The tell is a team celebrating a follower count or a raw database size while nobody can say what proportion is consented under current law, deliverable through current registration regimes, and identity-resolved to a paying account. The obvious reading — bigger list, bigger asset — is wrong because under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act and current messaging rules, an unconsented or unregistered contact has a reachability value of exactly zero, and in some cases a negative one.

7. How the picture changes by product type and stage

Some of the differences across product types are real and structural; some are folklore. It is worth separating them.

Stage changes the picture at least as much as category. A pre-product-market-fit company should treat nearly all paid spend as research cost, because the purpose is not to acquire customers economically but to discover which message and which audience produce any response at all; judging that spend on CAC is a category error, and so is asking it to build an owned asset it does not yet know the shape of. A company in its first scaling phase — Madhav's position — has the opposite problem: paid works, which is precisely why it is dangerous, because a working channel absorbs budget until its elasticity collapses and nobody notices, since the average CAC moves slowly even as the marginal one doubles. A mature company has accumulated owned assets and reputation, which lets it redirect paid from sustaining the base business toward defending share and launching new products; its characteristic failure is not over-spending but leaving owned assets unmaintained for years and then discovering that the "free" traffic has been melting at three per cent a month since 2022.

8. Three worked cases, including one that failed

Mandakini: building a channel that cannot be bought

Ira's answer to the board was not a mix. It was a construction project. With paid capable of producing perhaps sixteen placements a year at full share of voice, and the field team's capacity capped at roughly nine qualified evaluations per representative per year, the only path to 220 was to raise the conversion rate of evaluations, which meant attacking the credibility bottleneck directly. Mandakini funded fourteen structured method-comparison studies at customer sites — each costing about ₹4.2 lakh in reagents, engineer time and statistical support, ₹58.8 lakh in total — in which the analyser was run in parallel with the site's reference instrument across 400 patient samples, and the site retained the right to publish the results whether favourable or not. Nine sites published; two presented at a national pathology conference; the aggregate correlation data became a document the field team could leave behind. Over the following four quarters, evaluation-to-placement conversion rose from 9 per cent to 16 per cent, and the mean sales cycle shortened by 41 days. Placements reached 178 — short of 220, but achieved with commercial cost of ₹3.6 crore, which is a CAC of ₹2.02 lakh against the prior ₹3.02 lakh. In the framework's language, Mandakini spent money to raise k among a population of about 2,900 laboratory heads who talk to each other constantly. In plainer language, it bought evidence rather than attention.

Madhav: what the holdout changed, and what it did not

Sanjay's response to the 1.6-times incremental return was more restrained than his board expected. He did not cut paid; he capped it. Quarterly spend was held at ₹1.35 crore rather than the ₹2.1 crore in the plan, and brand-term bidding was reduced — not eliminated, because a competitor bidding on Madhav's brand name in two markets made complete withdrawal expensive, a fact only discovered by trying it for three weeks and watching signups fall 6 per cent in those markets while holding flat in the others. The ₹75 lakh released per quarter went to two places: a documentation and comparison-content team of three, on the view that owned elasticity was near 0.9 and therefore unsaturated, and a customer-evidence programme producing quantified deployment results. Eleven months later, self-serve signups attributed to non-paid sources had risen from 31 to 52 per cent of the total, blended CAC had fallen 24 per cent, and — the part Sanjay reported honestly to his board — total signup growth over the period was 19 per cent, below the 28 per cent the unconstrained paid plan had forecast. He argued, and his board accepted, that 19 per cent growth with a durable asset was worth more than 28 per cent rented, but the trade was real and he did not pretend otherwise.

Mitravinda: the failure, and what recovery actually required

Mitravinda Bazaar's story is the instructive one, because everything about its channel strategy was defensible and it still failed. In 2023 the company, a marketplace connecting handloom and handicraft producers in Rajasthan and Gujarat to urban buyers, concluded — correctly — that it could not win a paid auction against national horizontal marketplaces with vastly greater scale. It committed to an earned and community strategy: creator partnerships with textile-focused accounts, a documentary series about weaving clusters, a buyer community, an artisan-story programme. Over fourteen months it spent ₹2.1 crore. The content was genuinely good; two films were widely shared; follower counts rose from 40,000 to 380,000.

The reproduction number never exceeded 0.12. Measured properly — through referral codes, post-purchase surveys and a matched-cohort comparison — each acquired buyer generated about 0.12 additional buyers, against a threshold of roughly 0.28 at which the community function would have paid for itself. Orders grew 34 per cent over the period while spend implied a far higher expectation, and the company's cash position deteriorated sharply.

The diagnosis, when it finally came, was not about channels at all. Mitravinda's assortment averaged 2,400 live listings across 61 producer clusters, which meant a buyer who loved her first purchase and wanted to recommend the marketplace to a friend could not confidently say the friend would find something she wanted; repeat purchase within 180 days ran at 17 per cent. The company had spent ₹2.1 crore trying to increase transmission of a message that was not yet worth transmitting. The recovery took eighteen months and inverted the strategy: community spend was cut to near zero, ₹1.4 crore went into field operations that onboarded producers directly — an unglamorous, paid, negotiated channel — assortment reached 11,300 listings across 190 clusters, and 180-day repeat purchase rose to 39 per cent. Only then was the earned programme restarted, at a quarter of its former budget, and k measured 0.31, cutting effective CAC by 31 per cent. The lesson the team wrote into its own operating notes was blunt: earned reach amplifies product truth; when there is no truth worth amplifying, an earned budget is a very expensive way to find that out.

9. Failure modes, their early signs, and the cost of late detection

Six failure modes account for most of the damage this topic causes. Each has a characteristic early sign, a diagnostic question that catches it cheaply, and a cost that escalates steeply with delay.

10. Where competent experts genuinely disagree

Does paid create earned, or does earned merely get miscredited to paid? The mental-availability school holds that sustained paid reach builds memory structures that surface months later as direct traffic, branded search and apparently spontaneous recommendation; on this view, cutting brand spend produces a delayed collapse in "free" channels that no quarterly holdout will detect. Its evidence is the long-run econometric literature showing brand investment effects persisting over two to three years. The incrementalists reply that this is an unfalsifiable escape hatch: every disappointing test result is attributed to effects too long-dated to measure. What would have to be true for the brand school to be wrong is that geographies with sustained brand-spend reductions show no divergence in baseline demand over three years — a test few companies have the patience to run, though the ones that have run it report divergence in some categories and none in others, which is an uncomfortable answer for both sides.

Is owned media an asset or a liability? The taxonomists treat an email list, a content library and a community as capital. A sceptical minority — increasingly vocal since answer engines began absorbing informational traffic — argues that most owned properties have negative net present value once fully-loaded maintenance is counted, and that companies keep them for organisational rather than economic reasons. The sceptics' evidence is that when asked to produce the discounted calculation, most teams cannot, and when someone does it, the answer is frequently small or negative — Mitravinda's ₹34.5 lakh on a company with ₹70 crore of gross merchandise value is not a rounding error but it is close. What would have to be true for the sceptics to be wrong is that owned properties carry option value not captured in the cash-flow calculation: the ability to launch a new product to an existing audience, or to survive a paid-platform policy shock. That option value is real and nobody has a good way to price it.

Should earned be a funded function at all? One camp says yes: community, developer relations, public relations and customer advocacy are professional disciplines that reliably raise transmission when staffed well. The other says earned is strictly a by-product, that every rupee spent on it would earn more inside the product or the service, and that the existence of a community team mostly signals a company avoiding a harder conversation about its product. The strongest version of the by-product argument is Mitravinda's counterfactual: the ₹2.1 crore spent on transmission would have bought the assortment fix a year earlier. The strongest version of the funded-function argument is Mandakini's method-comparison programme, which was unmistakably an earned investment, cost ₹58.8 lakh, and moved conversion by seven percentage points. The two cases are reconcilable — one funded evidence, the other funded amplification — but the general rule that would separate them in advance has not been written down in a form practitioners agree on.

Is the answer-engine shift a threat to owned content or its vindication? One position holds that a content library whose purpose was to capture clicks is now stranded capital, and that budget should move to product surfaces and to paid, where inventory still exists. The opposing position holds that being cited is worth more than being clicked, since a citation carries third-party endorsement at the moment of decision, and that the companies writing the clearest, most structured, most verifiable documentation will own a new earned surface cheaply. Both positions are held by serious people and neither has more than eighteen months of data. What would settle it is a measurable relationship between citation share and revenue, at a company that has instrumented both — and in 2026, no such measurement has been published in a form the field trusts.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this topic can name three families and describe the control–cost–credibility trade. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in six observable ways. They ask what kind of object a proposed channel is before asking what it costs, because the answer determines whether to evaluate it on payback, on asset value, or on multiplier effect. They treat the elasticity, not the average CAC, as the number that governs the next decision, and they are willing to spend money deliberately degrading a working channel in order to measure it. They will not accept a plan whose target exceeds the addressable inventory of the channel it relies on, and they will do that arithmetic in a meeting, out loud, in under two minutes. They look at earned movements and check the release log before checking the community budget. They run the discounted value of every owned property annually and are willing to close one. And — the hardest one — they can distinguish between a channel problem and a product problem under commercial pressure, which usually means telling a board that the answer to a growth shortfall is not a new channel but eighteen months of assortment work, and being right about it often enough to be believed the next time.

12. What Ira and Sanjay decided

Ira Deshmukh did not build a channel mix. She told the Mandakini board that paid media in her category was capable of roughly sixteen placements a year at any budget she could justify, produced the arithmetic, and asked instead for ₹58.8 lakh to fund fourteen independent site evaluations with publication rights retained by the customer — which meant accepting that some results might be unfavourable and public. The board approved it over one director's objection that the company was "funding its competitors' evidence too". Her reasoning was that in a market of 2,900 buyers who confer constantly, the binding constraint was not reach but proof, and that proof is the only input that raises transmission in a professional network. She missed the 220 target and delivered 178 at a third lower acquisition cost, and the evaluation programme became a standing line item.

Sanjay Raghavan capped paid rather than cutting it, redirected ₹75 lakh a quarter into documentation and quantified customer evidence, and — the decision his team found hardest — instituted a standing quarterly holdout in two rotating geographies as a permanent cost of doing business, roughly ₹40 lakh a year of deliberately foregone spend. He accepted slower headline growth for a measured cost structure, and he told his board explicitly that if the answer-engine citation channel turned out to be purchasable within two years, he would have over-invested in documentation and would say so.

Discussion questions.
1. Mandakini's evaluation programme cost ₹58.8 lakh and produced publishable results the company could not control, including two that were merely adequate. Was that an earned-media investment, a product investment, or a form of paid media in which the currency was risk rather than cash — and does the classification change what the board should have demanded in return?
2. Sanjay's holdout showed a measured return of 1.6 times against a reported 4.1. Suppose his board had instead chosen to keep the old attribution model on the grounds that it had funded three years of growth. Construct the strongest defensible argument for that position, and identify the one piece of evidence that would defeat it.
3. Mitravinda spent ₹2.1 crore raising transmission of a proposition that was not yet worth transmitting. At what point in those fourteen months was the error detectable with data the company already had, and what would a competent observer have had to believe in order to keep funding it past that point?
